The name refers to reducing disorder between copies. It was described in work on replicated databases at Xerox PARC by Demers and colleagues in 1987.

Anti-entropy is the backstop among the convergence mechanisms in an [eventually consistent](node:Eventual%20consistency) store, since it covers data the others miss:

| Mechanism                               | When it runs               | What it covers               | Gap                        |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| [Hinted handoff](node:Hinted%20handoff) | When a replica returns     | Writes during a short outage | Lost hints, long outages   |
| [Read repair](node:Read%20repair)       | During reads               | Keys that are read           | Data nobody reads          |
| Anti-entropy                            | On a schedule or on demand | All data in scope            | Uses disk, CPU and network |

Comparing full datasets over the network would be too expensive, so implementations exchange summaries. A [Merkle tree](node:Merkle%20tree) lets two replicas locate differing key ranges by exchanging a small number of hashes, then transfer only those ranges. Exchanges can push data, pull data, or do both.

Repair frequency has a correctness consequence around deletes. Replicated stores usually record a delete as a tombstone (a marker saying the key was deleted) and purge it after a retention period. If a replica misses the delete and repair does not run before the tombstone is purged, that replica still holds the old row and no marker exists to override it. The next repair copies the row back to the others, and deleted data reappears. In Cassandra, for this reason, repair must complete within the `gc_grace_seconds` window.

Repairs are heavy operations, so schedule them with limits and stagger them across nodes. Run one after any outage longer than the hint window, and alert when a scheduled repair has not completed.
quotes: Customers deleted those records last month, and now they're back.
Sounds like tombstones expired before anti-entropy reached that replica. When did repair last finish on this cluster?

nodes.name: Merkle tree
nodes.description: A tree of hashes that lets two parties find which parts of large datasets differ by exchanging only a few hashes.
nodes.markdown:
A tree of hashes in which each leaf is the hash of a block of data and each parent is the hash of its children. The root therefore summarizes the entire dataset, and any change to a block changes every hash on the path up to the root. Ralph Merkle devised the structure around 1979.

In a [distributed system](node:Distributed%20system), Merkle trees answer a specific question: which parts of two large datasets differ? Sending all the data, or even all the keys, between replicas ([nodes](node:Node) holding copies) would consume a large amount of bandwidth just to confirm they mostly match. Two nodes can instead compare trees from the top down:

| Step | What happens                                                 |
| ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1    | Each node builds a tree over the same key ranges             |
| 2    | The nodes compare root hashes. If equal, the ranges match    |
| 3    | If different, they compare the hashes of the root's children |
| 4    | They descend only into subtrees whose hashes differ          |
| 5    | At the leaves, they exchange the data for mismatched ranges  |

If only one leaf differs, the comparison follows a single path, so the number of levels visited grows with the logarithm of the number of leaves. This is why [anti-entropy](node:Anti-entropy) in stores such as Dynamo and Cassandra uses these trees. Git and blockchains use the same structure or close variants.

Matching hashes indicate matching data with overwhelming probability, not certainty.

Tree granularity is a practical trade-off. If each leaf covers many keys, the tree stays small, but one differing key forces the whole range to be transferred, a problem called overstreaming. It shows up as a repair moving more data than differed. More leaves reduce that waste and use more memory.
quotes: Repair streamed 200 GB, but only a few thousand rows were out of sync.
The Merkle tree leaves are too coarse, so one bad key resends the whole range. Try increasing the tree depth on that table.

nodes.name: Gossip protocol
nodes.description: Nodes periodically exchange state with random peers, so information spreads through a cluster like an epidemic.
nodes.markdown:
A communication method in which each [node](node:Node) periodically exchanges information with a few randomly chosen peers. Those peers pass it on in later rounds, so an update spreads through the cluster the way an infection spreads through a population. These are also called epidemic protocols.

Each round, a node picks one or a few peers and does one of the following:

| Style     | What is exchanged                               |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Push      | The node sends the peer what it knows           |
| Pull      | The node asks the peer for what it is missing   |
| Push-pull | Both sides send each other what the other lacks |

Because the number of informed nodes grows roughly exponentially at first, an update reaches all N nodes in about O(log N) rounds with high probability. Each node sends a fixed amount per round, and there is no central coordinator. Random peer selection also routes around failed nodes and many [network partitions](node:Network%20partition) that are not complete.

Gossip commonly carries cluster membership, node health and metadata such as which node owns which data. Cassandra and Consul are examples. It often feeds a [failure detector](node:Failure%20detector), since peers can report on nodes they have heard from recently.

The trade-off is that delivery is probabilistic and delayed, giving [eventual consistency](node:Eventual%20consistency) for the gossiped state. During a rollout, different nodes can briefly hold different views of the cluster, so one routes a request to a member that another already considers gone.

Removals need particular care. A node that was removed can reappear because a peer still holds its old entry and gossips it back. Protocols prevent this by attaching a generation or version number to each entry, and by keeping a removal marker long enough for it to spread everywhere.
quotes: We decommissioned that node an hour ago, but it keeps showing up in the member list.
A peer's still gossiping its old state. Check that the removal marker has propagated before restarting anything.

nodes.name: Last-write-wins
nodes.description: A conflict rule that keeps the write with the highest timestamp and silently discards the others.
nodes.markdown:
A conflict resolution rule that keeps the write with the highest timestamp and discards the others. When replicas (the [nodes](node:Node) holding copies of a key) hold different versions, each compares timestamps and retains the winner, with a tie-breaker such as node ID. Every replica applies the same rule, so all converge on one value. This gives [eventual consistency](node:Eventual%20consistency) with little machinery, and it is the default in stores such as Cassandra.

The rule's weakness is that "last" means highest timestamp, which may not be the most recent write. With [clock skew](node:Clock%20skew), an older write can beat a newer one:

| Real order           | Node | Node's clock | Write            |
| -------------------- | ---- | ------------ | ---------------- |
| First                | A    | 10:00:00.300 | `status = "old"` |
| Second, 100 ms later | B    | 10:00:00.100 | `status = "new"` |

Node A's clock runs 300 ms ahead, so its earlier write has the higher timestamp. The store keeps `"old"`, and the write of `"new"` disappears even though its client received a success.

The rule also loses data when clocks are perfect. If two users edit a record concurrently, in the [happens-before](node:Happens-before) sense, then neither saw the other's change, and one edit is dropped with no error. Whole-record writes make it worse: two users changing different fields overwrite each other's work.

Several measures reduce the risk:

- Store each field separately, so edits to different fields do not conflict.
- Use immutable records with unique keys, so no two writes target the same key.
- Use compare-and-set (write only if the value is unchanged) where a lost update is unacceptable.
- Use a [hybrid logical clock](node:Hybrid%20logical%20clock), so a causally later write gets a higher timestamp.
- Use a [CRDT](node:CRDT) or a [vector clock](node:Vector%20clock) when concurrent updates must be preserved.
quotes: Support says two agents updated the ticket, and one note is gone.
The store uses last-write-wins on the whole row, so the second save replaced the first. We should move notes into their own records.

nodes.name: CRDT
nodes.description: Conflict-free replicated data type. A structure whose replicas can update independently and always merge to the same state.
nodes.markdown:
Conflict-free replicated data type: a data structure whose copies can be updated independently, with no coordination, and that converge when they exchange updates. Marc Shapiro and colleagues formalized the idea in 2011. The guarantee is called strong [eventual consistency](node:Eventual%20consistency): any two replicas (the [nodes](node:Node) holding copies) that have received the same set of updates are in the same state.

State-based CRDTs send their state and merge it with a commutative, associative and idempotent function, so messages can repeat or arrive in any order, which suits [at-least-once delivery](node:At-least-once%20delivery). Operation-based CRDTs send individual operations that commute when concurrent, and rely on a delivery layer that delivers each one once and, for many types, in causal order.

| Type         | Supports             | How it merges                                                                                     |
| ------------ | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| G-Counter    | Increment            | One count per node, merged by taking each maximum                                                 |
| PN-Counter   | Increment, decrement | Two G-Counters, value is increments minus decrements                                              |
| OR-Set       | Add, remove          | Each add gets a unique tag, and remove deletes only the tags it saw, so a concurrent add survives |
| LWW-Register | Set a value          | Highest timestamp wins, as in [last-write-wins](node:Last-write-wins)                             |

CRDTs fit collaborative editing and offline-first apps, where a user keeps working during a [network partition](node:Network%20partition) and merges later. Automerge and Yjs are examples of libraries.

Convergence does not mean the merged result is what users wanted. Two people editing one sentence can produce an interleaved result that is valid but unreadable. A plain CRDT also cannot enforce global invariants, such as "balance never goes below zero" or "usernames are unique", because each replica accepts updates before hearing from the others. Those checks need [consensus](node:Consensus) or quotas allocated to each replica in advance.
quotes: Can we make the inventory count a CRDT so warehouses can work offline?
The count would converge, but two warehouses could both sell the last unit. A plain counter CRDT can't enforce stock never going negative.

nodes.name: Consensus
nodes.description: The problem of getting a group of nodes to agree on one value, and never change it, even when some of them fail.
nodes.markdown:
The problem of getting a group of [nodes](node:Node) to agree on a single value, even when some of them fail. Once the value is decided, it stays decided. A standard formal definition has three properties:

| Property    | Requirement                                  | Type     |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| Agreement   | No two correct nodes decide different values | Safety   |
| Validity    | The decided value was proposed by some node  | Safety   |
| Termination | Every correct node eventually decides        | Liveness |

A safety property says nothing bad ever happens, and a liveness property says something good eventually happens. [FLP impossibility](node:FLP%20impossibility) shows that a deterministic protocol cannot guarantee both in a fully asynchronous network with even one crash. Practical protocols such as [Paxos](node:Paxos) and [Raft](node:Raft) therefore always preserve safety and rely on timing assumptions only for progress.

Many coordination tasks reduce to consensus: [leader election](node:Leader%20election), agreeing on cluster membership, deciding a transaction's outcome, and ordering commands in [state machine replication](node:State%20machine%20replication). Repeating consensus for each slot of a log yields total order broadcast (delivering the same messages to all nodes in the same order), and the two problems are equivalent in the [crash failure](node:Crash%20failure) model.

Tolerating f crash failures takes 2f + 1 nodes, because each decision needs a majority [quorum](node:Quorum) and any two majorities overlap.

When a three-node etcd cluster loses two members, the survivor stops accepting writes even though it is running. It cannot tell a crash from a [network partition](node:Network%20partition), and accepting writes could create a conflicting history. The protocol stops making progress so that it never disagrees with itself.

Each decision costs network round trips and durable disk writes, and adding voters adds to that cost. Systems therefore keep the voting group small and use it for metadata and coordination, with bulk data stored elsewhere.
quotes: Why not run a two-node etcd cluster? It's cheaper than three.
A majority of two is two, so losing either node stops consensus. You'd pay for a second machine and tolerate zero failures.

nodes.name: FLP impossibility
nodes.description: No deterministic protocol can guarantee consensus in an asynchronous system if even one node may crash.
nodes.markdown:
A proof that no deterministic algorithm can guarantee [consensus](node:Consensus) in a fully asynchronous system if even one process may crash. It is named after Michael Fischer, Nancy Lynch and Michael Paterson, who published it in 1985.

The result depends on its exact assumptions:

| Assumption       | Meaning in the proof                                                  |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Asynchronous     | No bound on message delay or relative processing speed, and no clocks |
| Reliable network | Every message is eventually delivered, exactly once                   |
| One crash        | At most one process may stop, at any point                            |
| Deterministic    | Each step is fully determined by a process's state and input          |
| Nontrivial       | Both possible decision values can be reached                          |

The difficulty comes from a process being unable to tell a crashed peer from a slow one. The proof shows that any such protocol has an initial state from which the outcome is not yet fixed, and that an adversarial schedule of message deliveries can keep it undecided forever.

FLP does not say consensus is unachievable in practice. It says no protocol in this model can guarantee termination in every possible execution. The non-terminating schedules can be made unlikely, and systems escape the result by changing an assumption:

| Approach                                    | Added assumption                                                    | Example                                |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Partial synchrony                           | The network eventually behaves within time bounds                   | [Paxos](node:Paxos), [Raft](node:Raft) |
| Randomization                               | [Nodes](node:Node) use coin flips, and terminate with probability 1 | Ben-Or's 1983 algorithm                |
| [Failure detector](node:Failure%20detector) | An oracle that is eventually accurate enough                        | Chandra-Toueg algorithm                |

The practical consequence appears in how Raft and Paxos fail. Under bad timing, such as repeated [leader election](node:Leader%20election) rounds on an unstable network, a cluster may stop making progress for as long as the instability lasts. It will not return conflicting decisions.
quotes: Can we prove our election always finishes within some time limit?
Not on an asynchronous network. FLP rules out guaranteed termination. We can prove it never elects two leaders per term, and use randomized timeouts so it converges in practice.

nodes.name: Paxos
nodes.description: Lamport's consensus protocol, in which proposers and a majority of acceptors choose one value in two phases.
nodes.markdown:
A [consensus](node:Consensus) protocol devised by Leslie Lamport and published in 1998. It lets a group of [nodes](node:Node) choose one value while tolerating [crash failures](node:Crash%20failure) of a minority, message loss and message delay.

Paxos defines three roles, and one server often plays all of them:

- Proposers suggest values.
- Acceptors vote on proposals.
- Learners find out which value was chosen.

Single-decree Paxos decides one value in two phases:

| Phase       | From → to            | What happens                                                                                                                                            |
| ----------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1a Prepare  | Proposer → acceptors | Proposer picks a unique number `n` and sends `prepare(n)`                                                                                               |
| 1b Promise  | Acceptor → proposer  | If `n` is above any prepare it has answered, the acceptor promises to ignore lower numbers and returns the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted    |
| 2a Accept   | Proposer → acceptors | With promises from a majority, proposer sends `accept(n, v)`. `v` must be the value of the highest-numbered proposal returned, or its own value if none |
| 2b Accepted | Acceptor → learners  | Acceptor accepts unless it has promised a number above `n`                                                                                              |

A value is chosen once a majority of acceptors have accepted the same proposal. The rule in step 2a provides safety: any later proposer must learn of a possibly chosen value through the overlapping [quorum](node:Quorum) and propose it again. Acceptors must persist promises and acceptances to disk before replying, or a restart could break those promises.

Two proposers can block each other indefinitely by issuing ever-higher numbers, each invalidating the other's phase 1. A distinguished leader or randomized backoff makes this livelock unlikely.

Real systems need a sequence of decisions for [state machine replication](node:State%20machine%20replication). Multi-Paxos runs one instance per log slot, and a stable leader can skip phase 1 for later slots. [Raft](node:Raft) was designed partly because the original papers leave these engineering details open.
quotes: Throughput dropped to nothing and both servers are busy sending prepares.
Dueling proposers, preempting each other in phase 1. Add a stable leader or randomized backoff.

nodes.name: Raft
nodes.description: A leader-based consensus protocol for replicating a log, designed to be easier to understand than Paxos.
nodes.markdown:
A [consensus](node:Consensus) protocol for maintaining a replicated log, published by Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout in 2014 with understandability as an explicit goal. It provides fault tolerance comparable to Multi-[Paxos](node:Paxos), and etcd and Consul use it.

Each [node](node:Node) is in one of three roles:

| Role      | What it does                                                                     |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Follower  | Responds to requests, and starts an election if it hears no leader               |
| Candidate | Increments the term, votes for itself and requests votes                         |
| Leader    | Handles client writes, replicates the log and sends [heartbeats](node:Heartbeat) |

Time is divided into numbered terms, and each term has at most one leader. A follower whose randomized election timeout expires becomes a candidate. It wins with votes from a majority [quorum](node:Quorum), and each node casts at most one vote per term, recorded on disk. A voter refuses any candidate whose log is less up to date than its own, so a new leader always holds every committed entry.

The leader appends each command to its log and sends it to followers with AppendEntries messages, which include the index and term of the preceding entry so followers can reject mismatches. An entry from the current term is committed once a majority stores it. Entries from earlier terms become committed only indirectly, when a later entry from the current term commits. Committed entries are applied in order, as in [state machine replication](node:State%20machine%20replication).

A common operational problem is election churn. If disk or network latency delays heartbeats past the election timeout, followers keep starting elections, and writes stall even though every node is up. Raising the timeout or moving the log to a faster disk usually helps.

A deposed leader may not know it has been replaced, so linearizable reads must confirm leadership first.
quotes: etcd keeps logging leader changes, but all three members are up.
Check disk sync latency. If the disk stalls, Raft heartbeats miss the election timeout and followers call new elections.

nodes.name: Leader election
nodes.description: The process by which a group of nodes chooses one to coordinate work, and replaces it when it fails.
nodes.markdown:
The process by which a group of [nodes](node:Node) chooses one member to coordinate work, and chooses a replacement when that member fails. A single leader can order writes, assign tasks or run a scheduled job without negotiating each decision.

An election protocol has two goals. Safety means at most one leader is recognized for a given term (a numbered period of leadership). Liveness means that a leader is eventually chosen as long as enough nodes are working. [FLP impossibility](node:FLP%20impossibility) means liveness cannot be guaranteed on a fully asynchronous network, so protocols depend on timeouts.

| Approach                         | How a leader is chosen                                                        | Safe under partition?            |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| [Consensus](node:Consensus) vote | A majority votes in a numbered term, as in [Raft](node:Raft)                  | Yes, one leader per term         |
| Coordination service             | Nodes compete for a [lease](node:Lease) in a system such as etcd or ZooKeeper | Yes, if stale leaders are fenced |
| Bully algorithm                  | The highest-ID reachable node wins                                            | No, each side can elect its own  |
| Manual or static                 | An operator or config file names the leader                                   | Depends on the operator          |

A correct election does not ensure that only one node believes it is leader at every moment. A leader that pauses or loses contact can continue acting on an old belief while a new leader is elected. The guarantee is per term, and that gap is how [split brain](node:Split%20brain) reaches external systems. When a leader writes to shared storage, protect the write with a [fencing token](node:Fencing%20token), such as the term number.

Elections also cost availability. Between the old leader failing and a new one taking over, writes fail or hang, typically for the detection timeout plus the election itself. Timeouts set too aggressively cause repeated elections under load, when a [failure detector](node:Failure%20detector) mistakes slowness for failure.
quotes: The cron job ran twice last night, once on each scheduler.
The old scheduler was paused during the handover and woke up still thinking it led. The job needs a fencing check.

nodes.name: Lease
nodes.description: A time-limited grant of a right or resource, which expires automatically unless the holder renews it.
nodes.markdown:
A time-limited grant of a right, such as being leader or holding a lock, that expires automatically unless the holder renews it. Cary Gray and David Cheriton described leases in 1989 for file cache consistency. If a [node](node:Node) holding an ordinary lock crashes, the lock may never be released. A lease ends on its own.

| Step | Who     | What happens                                                      |
| ---- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Holder  | Records its local time, then requests a lease of duration D       |
| 2    | Grantor | Grants the lease and starts timing D                              |
| 3    | Holder  | Works, and renews well before D runs out                          |
| 4    | Holder  | Stops work if it cannot renew by its local expiry                 |
| 5    | Grantor | After D plus a safety margin, may grant the lease to another node |

The holder starts counting before sending its request, so its expiry falls earlier than the grantor's. This keeps the two views safe without synchronized wall clocks, provided [clock drift](node:Clock%20drift) stays below an assumed bound. Durations should use a monotonic clock (a timer that only moves forward).

Lease duration is a trade-off. A short lease recovers faster after a crash but needs more renewal traffic and is easier to lose in a brief stall.

A paused holder can outlive its lease. A process checks its lease, sees it is valid, and is then paused by garbage collection (the runtime halting the program to reclaim memory) or a VM migration. The lease expires, another node acquires it, and the first process wakes and carries on with its write. No check inside the process can close this gap, since the pause can land right after the check. Protecting the resource takes a [fencing token](node:Fencing%20token).
quotes: Worker A's lease expired during a long GC pause, and it still wrote to the bucket.
A lease can't stop that by itself. The storage layer has to reject stale holders, so let's add a fencing token.

nodes.name: Distributed lock
nodes.description: A lock shared across machines so only one holder acts at a time. It cannot guarantee that alone when holders can pause.
nodes.markdown:
A lock that coordinates processes on different machines, so that only one of them works on a resource at a time. Because a holder can crash without releasing it, a distributed lock is almost always implemented as a [lease](node:Lease) that expires. That expiry is the source of its main weakness: a holder can lose the lock without knowing.

The typical incident looks like this. Worker A acquires the lock and stalls, perhaps in a garbage collection pause (the runtime halting to reclaim memory). Its lease expires. Worker B acquires the lock and starts writing. Worker A resumes, still believing it holds the lock, and also writes. The same job has run twice or a file is corrupted, even though the locking code contains no bug.

The right lock depends on its purpose:

| Purpose     | If two holders overlap             | Suitable approach                                                                                            |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Efficiency  | Some work is duplicated            | A simple lock, such as Redis `SET key value NX PX ttl`                                                       |
| Correctness | Data is corrupted or money is lost | A [consensus](node:Consensus)-backed lock in etcd or ZooKeeper, plus a [fencing token](node:Fencing%20token) |

A lock on a single [node](node:Node) is unavailable or lost if that node fails, and failover with asynchronous replication can grant the same lock twice. A consensus-backed service avoids that but cannot stop a paused client. Only the protected resource can, by rejecting stale requests.

Give each acquisition a unique value and release only if the stored value still matches, or a slow worker can delete a lock now held by someone else. Where possible, avoid the lock altogether by using [idempotency](node:Idempotency) or a compare-and-set write (a write that succeeds only if the value is unchanged), which puts the check at the resource.
quotes: We put a Redis lock around the invoice job and still got duplicates.
A lock only narrows that window. If the worker pauses past the expiry, two can run. Make the invoice insert idempotent.

nodes.name: Fencing token
nodes.description: An increasing number issued with each lock grant, letting a resource reject writes from a holder that has been replaced.
nodes.markdown:
A number that increases with every grant of a [lease](node:Lease) or lock, which the holder attaches to each request to the protected resource. The resource remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects anything lower. This stops a former holder that does not yet know it has been replaced.

Fencing addresses the gap that a [distributed lock](node:Distributed%20lock) cannot close on its own, because a client can pause at any moment and resume after its lease has expired:

| Step | Actor    | Action                                  | Storage's highest token |
| ---- | -------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| 1    | Client 1 | Acquires lock, receives token 33        | 32                      |
| 2    | Client 1 | Pauses, and its lease expires           | 32                      |
| 3    | Client 2 | Acquires lock, receives token 34        | 32                      |
| 4    | Client 2 | Writes with token 34, accepted          | 34                      |
| 5    | Client 1 | Resumes, writes with token 33, rejected | 34                      |

Without step 5's check, Client 1 would overwrite Client 2's work, and neither client would see an error.

Two requirements make this work. The tokens must come from a source that never gives one number to two holders or goes backward, which in practice means a system built on [consensus](node:Consensus). A [Raft](node:Raft) term, an etcd revision and a ZooKeeper transaction ID (zxid) are common sources. The resource must also perform the comparison and the write atomically, because a separate check followed by a write reopens the race.

The second requirement is the practical limit. Fencing needs the resource to participate, and many do not. A database can do it with a conditional update such as `UPDATE ... WHERE fence_token <= 34`. A third-party API usually cannot, so for those calls use an [idempotency](node:Idempotency) key (a unique ID that lets the receiver discard repeats) and accept that the protection is weaker.
quotes: The old leader came back after the pause and overwrote the new leader's output.
Nothing was checking who was current. Pass the term as a fencing token and have storage reject anything lower than it's seen.

nodes.name: Two-phase commit
nodes.description: A protocol that makes a transaction commit on all participants or none, but can block if the coordinator fails.
nodes.markdown:
A protocol that makes a transaction across several [nodes](node:Node) either commit on all of them or abort on all of them. One node acts as coordinator and the others are participants. It is often shortened to 2PC, and differs from two-phase locking, a technique for isolating concurrent transactions.

| Step | Who         | What happens                                                                       |
| ---- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Coordinator | Sends prepare to all participants                                                  |
| 2    | Participant | Durably records its changes and vote, keeps its locks, and replies yes or no       |
| 3    | Coordinator | Decides commit if all voted yes, otherwise abort, and records the decision durably |
| 4    | Coordinator | Sends the decision to all participants                                             |
| 5    | Participant | Applies the decision, releases locks and acknowledges                              |

A yes vote is binding. The participant must be able to commit even after a crash and restart, and it may not decide alone.

That promise creates the protocol's known weakness. If the coordinator fails after participants vote yes but before they hear the decision, they are in doubt. They cannot commit, because another participant may have voted no. They cannot abort, because the coordinator may have decided to commit. So they wait, holding locks, and other transactions touching those rows queue behind them. The symptom is a table that appears frozen with no active query to blame, until the coordinator recovers or an operator intervenes.

2PC is not a [consensus](node:Consensus) protocol in the fault-tolerant sense. It requires every participant to respond, so one failure can stop progress, where consensus needs only a majority. A common remedy combines the two: each participant and the coordinator are replicated with [Paxos](node:Paxos) or [Raft](node:Raft), so that a single machine failure cannot leave a transaction stuck. Spanner uses this design. [Three-phase commit](node:Three-phase%20commit) tried a different remedy.
quotes: This table has been locked for an hour, but nothing's running.
Check pg_prepared_xacts. It's likely an in-doubt two-phase commit whose coordinator died. Get the outcome from the coordinator's log before resolving it.

nodes.name: Three-phase commit
nodes.description: A variant of two-phase commit that avoids blocking under crash failures, but can break atomicity during a partition.
nodes.markdown:
A variant of [two-phase commit](node:Two-phase%20commit) that adds a phase to avoid blocking when the coordinator crashes. Dale Skeen proposed it in the early 1980s. It is often shortened to 3PC.

Two-phase commit blocks because a participant that voted yes cannot tell whether anyone has already committed. Three-phase commit removes that uncertainty by inserting a step between voting and committing:

| Phase        | Coordinator                                      | Participants                                |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| 1. CanCommit | Asks whether each can commit                     | Vote yes or no                              |
| 2. PreCommit | If all voted yes, announces the intent to commit | Record the pre-commit state and acknowledge |
| 3. DoCommit  | After all acknowledge, tells them to commit      | Commit and acknowledge                      |

The added phase creates a useful invariant: no participant commits until every participant has voted yes and has been told so. If the coordinator crashes, the surviving participants can elect a new one and inspect their states. If any of them reached pre-commit, every participant voted yes, so they can finish the commit. If none did, nobody can have committed, so they can safely abort.

That recovery requires [crash failures](node:Crash%20failure) only, bounded message delays, and a reliable [failure detector](node:Failure%20detector), so that a slow [node](node:Node) is never mistaken for a dead one.

Under a [network partition](node:Network%20partition), the protocol can break atomicity, its main guarantee. Suppose participants that received pre-commit end up on one side and the rest on the other. The first group commits, the second sees no pre-commit and aborts, and the transaction ends up committed on some nodes and aborted on others. Two-phase commit would have blocked here and preserved atomicity.

Production systems that need non-blocking commit usually run two-phase commit over groups replicated with [consensus](node:Consensus), using [Paxos](node:Paxos) or [Raft](node:Raft).
quotes: Couldn't we switch to three-phase commit so a dead coordinator stops blocking us?
Only if the network never partitions. Otherwise each side can decide differently. Replicating the coordinator with Raft is safer.

nodes.name: At-most-once delivery
nodes.description: A guarantee that a message is processed zero or one times. It is never duplicated, but it can be lost.
nodes.markdown:
A delivery guarantee in which each message is processed zero or one times. A message is never handled twice, but it can be lost. The sender makes one attempt, or the receiver records progress before doing the work, so that a failure leaves the message unprocessed and nothing tries again.

The guarantee is a consequence of the same ambiguity behind every [partial failure](node:Partial%20failure). If a sender gets no acknowledgment, it cannot know whether the message arrived. It must choose between resending, which risks a duplicate, and not resending, which risks a loss. At-most-once chooses not to resend. [At-least-once delivery](node:At-least-once%20delivery) makes the opposite choice.

In a message queue, the order of two consumer steps determines which guarantee you get:

| Step | At-most-once consumer | If it crashes right after this step        |
| ---- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| 1    | Receives the message  | Message is redelivered, nothing lost       |
| 2    | Commits its position  | Message is lost, because it counts as done |
| 3    | Processes the message | Work is complete                           |

The symptom is a gap: a queue dashboard shows everything consumed and no errors, yet some records never reached the destination, often clustered around a deployment or crash. Auto-commit settings in consumer libraries can produce this behavior without anyone having chosen it, since the position may be committed on a timer while work is still in progress.

At-most-once suits data where a small loss costs less than a duplicate or a retry: high-volume metrics, debug logs, telemetry samples, or live position updates that the next message replaces anyway.

It does not suit payments, orders, or anything that must eventually happen. If a loss is unacceptable, use at-least-once delivery with [idempotency](node:Idempotency), which together produce [exactly-once semantics](node:Exactly-once%20semantics).
quotes: We lost about forty events during the last deploy, but the consumer shows no errors.
It auto-commits offsets before processing finishes, so that's at-most-once delivery. Commit after the work is done.

nodes.name: At-least-once delivery
nodes.description: A guarantee that a message is retried until acknowledged. It will not be lost, but it may be processed more than once.
nodes.markdown:
A delivery guarantee in which a message is retried until the receiver acknowledges it. As long as the sender keeps running or has stored the message durably, and the receiver eventually recovers, the message is not lost. It may be processed more than once, which is the trade-off against [at-most-once delivery](node:At-most-once%20delivery).

Duplicates are an inherent part of this guarantee, because of [partial failure](node:Partial%20failure). When an acknowledgment is lost, the sender cannot distinguish that case from the message itself being lost, so it sends again:

| Step | Who      | What happens                                                            |
| ---- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Sender   | Stores the message and sends it                                         |
| 2    | Receiver | Processes the message                                                   |
| 3    | Receiver | Sends an acknowledgment, which is lost or never sent because of a crash |
| 4    | Sender   | Times out with no acknowledgment                                        |
| 5    | Sender   | Resends the message                                                     |
| 6    | Receiver | Processes the same message a second time                                |

The result is a recognizable class of bug: a customer gets two confirmation emails, an account is charged twice, or a counter runs higher than the true value. These often appear in clusters after a deployment or a broker failover, when many in-flight messages are redelivered together.

The fix belongs in the receiver. Make processing safe to repeat through [idempotency](node:Idempotency), typically by recording each message ID in the same database transaction as the work. This combination is how systems usually achieve [exactly-once semantics](node:Exactly-once%20semantics).

Retries introduce two other problems. A malformed message that always fails will be redelivered forever and can block a queue, so after a limited number of attempts it should move to a dead-letter queue (a holding area for messages needing inspection). Retries can also reorder messages, so consumers that depend on order must check a version or sequence number.
quotes: A few customers got the shipping email twice after last night's broker restart.
The queue is at-least-once, so redelivery is expected. The email worker needs to dedupe on message ID.

nodes.name: Exactly-once semantics
nodes.description: Each message's effect is applied once, usually by combining retries with deduplication or an atomic commit.
nodes.markdown:
A processing guarantee in which the effect of each message is applied exactly once, even if the message is transmitted several times. Over an unreliable network, no protocol can ensure that a message is physically delivered exactly once, because a sender that gets no acknowledgment cannot tell whether the message or the reply was lost. What systems can provide is an outcome equivalent to one delivery.

The standard construction is [at-least-once delivery](node:At-least-once%20delivery) plus a mechanism that makes repeats harmless. Retries ensure nothing is lost, and the receiver ensures duplicates have no further effect:

| Technique                       | How it works                                                              | Boundary of the guarantee        |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| [Idempotency](node:Idempotency) | The receiver records message IDs and ignores repeats                      | Wherever the IDs are stored      |
| Atomic position and result      | Result and consumer position commit in one database transaction           | That one database                |
| Broker transactions             | Kafka's transactions commit output messages and consumer offsets together | Topics within that Kafka cluster |

Every technique has a boundary, and bugs often come from crossing it. A stream processor may advertise exactly-once, and within its own state and topics that claim holds. If a handler also sends an email or calls a payment API, that side effect sits outside the transaction. When the handler crashes and is re-run, the email goes out again.

For an external call, pass an idempotency key that the third party honors. If it offers none, you must choose between possibly repeating the action and possibly missing it, as with any [partial failure](node:Partial%20failure).

Deduplication has limits. IDs are kept for a retention window, so a message redelivered after it is processed again. The ID check and the effect must also commit atomically, or a crash between them produces a duplicate or a loss.
quotes: Kafka is set to exactly-once, so why did the webhook fire twice?
That guarantee stops at Kafka. The webhook is an external side effect, so it needs its own idempotency key.

nodes.name: Idempotency
nodes.description: The property that performing an operation several times has the same effect as performing it once.
nodes.markdown:
The property that performing an operation several times has the same effect as performing it once. In a [distributed system](node:Distributed%20system), it makes retries safe. A timed-out request may or may not have been applied, as in any [partial failure](node:Partial%20failure), and the client can resend it without knowing which.

Whether an operation is idempotent depends on how it is expressed:

| Operation                                                | Idempotent? | Why                             |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------- |
| `SET balance = 100`                                      | Yes         | Repeating leaves the same value |
| `balance = balance + 10`                                 | No          | Each repeat adds 10             |
| `DELETE WHERE id = 7`                                    | Yes         | The row stays gone              |
| `INSERT` with a generated ID                             | No          | Each repeat creates a row       |
| `INSERT` with a client-chosen ID and a unique constraint | Yes         | Repeats are rejected or ignored |

Other operations can use an idempotency key, a unique ID the client generates once per logical operation and reuses on every retry. The server stores the key with the result, and on a repeat it returns that result and skips the work. Without this, a double-clicked pay button can charge a customer twice.

The key and the effect must commit in one transaction, or a crash between them breaks the guarantee. Concurrent retries can both pass a "have I seen this?" check, so enforce uniqueness with a database constraint. Keys are eventually deleted, so the retention period must exceed the longest time a client might retry.

Idempotent does not mean safe to replay at any time. If `SET x = 1` is delayed and retried after another client has run `SET x = 2`, the retry undoes the newer write. Guarding against that takes a version check or a [fencing token](node:Fencing%20token).

Idempotency is the receiver's half of [exactly-once semantics](node:Exactly-once%20semantics), paired with [at-least-once delivery](node:At-least-once%20delivery).
quotes: The mobile client retries on timeout, and we're seeing duplicate orders.
The create endpoint isn't idempotent. Have the client send a key and put a unique constraint on it.
